title: Vision & the Visual Pathway
summary: From retina to occipital cortex, and the field defects that localize lesions.

lessons.title: The Retina

levels.kid:
At the back of your eye is a thin layer called the retina. It works like the sensor in a camera.

The retina has two kinds of light catchers. Rods are great in the dark, but they only see in gray. Cones see colors and tiny details, but they need bright light.

In the very middle of the retina is a special spot packed with cones. That's the spot you use to read and look straight at things.

When light hits the light catchers, they turn it into nerve messages. The messages leave the eye through a cable called the optic nerve and travel to your brain. Your brain turns them into the picture you see!
levels.hs:
The **retina** is a thin sheet of neural tissue lining the back of the eye. It is actually part of the brain, grown out during development.

**Photoreceptors** turn light into electrical signals:
- **Rods**: very sensitive, work in dim light, no color, mostly in the peripheral retina. About 120 million.
- **Cones**: need brighter light, give **color** and **sharp detail**. Three types respond best to short (blue), medium (green) and long (red) wavelengths. About 6 million.

The **fovea**, at the center of the **macula**, has only cones packed tightly, giving the sharpest vision. The **optic disc**, where nerve fibers leave the eye, has no photoreceptors, so it creates a **blind spot**. Your brain fills it in.

Signals flow: **photoreceptors → bipolar cells → ganglion cells**. Horizontal and amacrine cells connect sideways and sharpen contrast. Ganglion cell axons form the **optic nerve**.

Odd fact: light must pass through all the other layers to reach photoreceptors at the very back.

Diseases:
- **Macular degeneration**: loss of central vision in older adults
- **Retinitis pigmentosa**: rods die first, causing night blindness and tunnel vision
- **Retinal detachment**: flashes, floaters and a curtain over vision; an emergency
- **Diabetic retinopathy**: damaged retinal blood vessels
levels.college:
**Layers** (from outside in): retinal pigment epithelium (RPE), photoreceptor outer segments, outer nuclear layer, outer plexiform layer, inner nuclear layer (bipolar, horizontal, amacrine cells), inner plexiform layer, ganglion cell layer, nerve fiber layer. Light crosses the inner layers to reach photoreceptors (inverted retina); at the fovea inner layers are displaced to reduce scatter.

**Phototransduction**: in darkness, cGMP-gated cation channels in outer segments are open (the **dark current**), so photoreceptors are depolarized and release glutamate continuously. A photon isomerizes **11-cis retinal to all-trans retinal**, activating the opsin (rhodopsin in rods), which activates the G protein **transducin**, which activates **phosphodiesterase 6**. cGMP falls, channels close, and the cell **hyperpolarizes**, reducing glutamate release. The RPE regenerates 11-cis retinal (visual cycle; vitamin A dependent).

**Bipolar cells**:
- **ON bipolar** cells use metabotropic **mGluR6** receptors; glutamate hyperpolarizes them, so they depolarize when light reduces glutamate.
- **OFF bipolar** cells use ionotropic AMPA/kainate receptors and depolarize in the dark.

**Center-surround receptive fields** arise via horizontal cell lateral inhibition, enhancing edges.

**Ganglion cell classes**:
- **Midget** (parvocellular): small fields, color (red-green), fine detail
- **Parasol** (magnocellular): large fields, motion, contrast
- **Small bistratified** (koniocellular): blue-yellow
- **Intrinsically photosensitive RGCs** (melanopsin): project to the suprachiasmatic nucleus (circadian rhythm) and pretectum (pupillary reflex)

**Convergence**: many rods converge on one ganglion cell (high sensitivity, poor acuity); foveal cones have nearly one-to-one connections (high acuity).

**Clinical**: central retinal artery occlusion causes sudden painless monocular blindness with a cherry-red spot and should be treated as a stroke. **Papilledema** is optic disc swelling from raised intracranial pressure.
levels.phd:
**Signal amplification and adaptation.** A single photoisomerization activates many transducin molecules and PDE6 enzymes, closing a measurable fraction of channels so that rods detect single photons. Shutoff requires rhodopsin kinase phosphorylation and arrestin binding; RGS9 accelerates transducin GTP hydrolysis. Calcium, entering through cGMP channels, provides negative feedback via guanylate cyclase-activating proteins: light lowers calcium, increasing cGMP synthesis and driving light adaptation across roughly ten log units of illumination.

**Parallel processing.** The retina contains more than a dozen bipolar types and around 40 ganglion cell types in mammals, each tiling the retina and sending a distinct feature map: direction-selective cells (computed by starburst amacrine cell asymmetric inhibition), object-motion detectors, local edge detectors and others. The image sent to the brain is therefore a set of parallel feature channels rather than a pixel map.

**Rod pathway.** Rods feed rod bipolar cells, which connect not directly to ganglion cells but to AII amacrine cells, which piggyback onto cone pathways via gap junctions (to ON cone bipolars) and glycinergic synapses (to OFF cone bipolars). This shared circuitry explains why congenital stationary night blindness caused by mGluR6 pathway mutations (e.g., TRPM1, NYX) produces a "negative" ERG with absent b-wave.

**Electroretinography** dissects layers: the a-wave reflects photoreceptor hyperpolarization; the b-wave reflects ON bipolar depolarization; oscillatory potentials reflect amacrine activity. Pattern ERG and optical coherence tomography (OCT) of ganglion cell and nerve fiber layers quantify neurodegeneration, and OCT thinning tracks axonal loss in multiple sclerosis.

**Therapeutics.** Voretigene neparvovec, an AAV2 vector delivering RPE65, was the first approved gene therapy for an inherited retinal disease. Optogenetic restoration (expressing a light-sensitive channelrhodopsin in ganglion cells of blind patients) has produced partial visual function, using the retina as a test bed for circuit-level neural repair.
levels.expert:
**The retina is a window to the brain**, and fundoscopy is a neurological exam skill.

**Papilledema**: bilateral optic disc swelling from raised intracranial pressure. Signs: blurred disc margins, obscured vessels at the margin, venous engorgement, loss of spontaneous venous pulsations (their presence makes elevated pressure less likely but doesn't exclude it), hemorrhages. Symptoms: headache worse lying down, transient visual obscurations, pulsatile tinnitus, and diplopia from sixth nerve palsy. Visual acuity is preserved early, but the blind spot enlarges and fields constrict; untreated, it causes permanent vision loss. Always image the brain (tumor, hydrocephalus, venous sinus thrombosis) before lumbar puncture. Idiopathic intracranial hypertension is a diagnosis of exclusion; refractory cases may need CSF shunting, venous sinus stenting or optic nerve sheath fenestration.

**Pseudopapilledema** (optic disc drusen, crowded discs) is a common mimic; OCT and ultrasound help, preventing unnecessary workups.

**Sudden monocular vision loss**:
- **Central retinal artery occlusion**: pale retina, cherry-red spot. A stroke equivalent: urgent stroke center referral, workup for carotid stenosis, cardiac embolism and, in older patients, **giant cell arteritis** (check ESR/CRP and start steroids promptly if suspected).
- **Amaurosis fugax**: transient monocular blindness, often embolic from the ipsilateral carotid; a warning for stroke.
- **Retinal detachment**: flashes, floaters, curtain; urgent ophthalmology.

**OCT in neurosurgery**: ganglion cell layer and nerve fiber layer thickness predict visual recovery after decompressing a pituitary tumor: preserved layers mean a better chance of recovery after surgery.

**Pitfall**: a dilated fundus exam needs pupil dilation, which removes the pupil exam temporarily. In a neurosurgical patient whose pupils are being monitored, never dilate without documenting it and agreeing with the team, or a dilated pupil may be mistaken for herniation.

keyPoints: Rods: dim light, no color, periphery, high convergence; cones: color and acuity, concentrated in the fovea
Photoreceptors hyperpolarize to light: rhodopsin → transducin → PDE6 → cGMP falls → channels close
ON bipolars (mGluR6) depolarize to light; OFF bipolars depolarize in darkness
Pathway: photoreceptors → bipolar cells → ganglion cells (axons form the optic nerve); horizontal/amacrine cells for lateral processing
Optic disc = blind spot; melanopsin ganglion cells drive circadian rhythm and pupil reflex
Papilledema = disc swelling from raised ICP; CRAO = cherry-red spot, a stroke equivalent

lessons.title: The Visual Pathway

levels.kid:
Each eye sends its pictures to the brain through a cable called the optic nerve.

The two cables meet behind your eyes in an X-shaped crossing. Some wires cross to the other side and some stay on the same side. After the crossing, everything you see on your left side goes to the right half of your brain, and everything on your right goes to the left half!

The wires stop at a relay station in the middle of the brain. Then they fan out all the way to the very back of your head. That back part is where seeing really happens.

So you see with your eyes AND the back of your head!
levels.hs:
Here is the route visual signals travel:

1. **Retina** → ganglion cell axons form the **optic nerve** (cranial nerve II).
2. **Optic chiasm**: the two optic nerves meet under the brain, just above the pituitary gland. Fibers from the **nasal** (inner) half of each retina **cross**. Fibers from the **temporal** (outer) half stay on the same side.
3. **Optic tract**: after the chiasm, each tract carries information about the **opposite visual field** from both eyes. The left optic tract carries everything you see to your right.
4. **Lateral geniculate nucleus (LGN)** of the thalamus: the relay station.
5. **Optic radiations**: fibers fan out through the temporal and parietal lobes. The lower fibers loop forward through the temporal lobe (**Meyer's loop**) and carry the upper visual field.
6. **Primary visual cortex (V1)** in the occipital lobe, along the **calcarine fissure**.

Why do nasal fibers cross? The nasal retina sees the temporal (outer) visual field. Crossing makes each brain half receive one whole side of the world.

After V1, information splits:
- The **"where/how" stream** goes up to the parietal lobe (motion, location)
- The **"what" stream** goes down to the temporal lobe (recognizing objects and faces)

Some optic fibers also go to the brainstem for pupil reflexes and eye orienting.
levels.college:
**Optic nerve**: about a million ganglion cell axons, myelinated by **oligodendrocytes** and wrapped in meninges, so it is CNS white matter (affected in MS and neuromyelitis optica; raised ICP transmits along its sheath). Segments: intraocular, intraorbital, intracanalicular, intracranial.

**Optic chiasm**: nasal retinal fibers decussate (a little over half of all fibers); it lies above the diaphragma sellae and pituitary, below the third ventricle, between the internal carotid arteries.

**Optic tract**: wraps around the cerebral peduncle to the LGN; also sends fibers to the **pretectum** (pupillary light reflex), **superior colliculus** (orienting, saccades) and **suprachiasmatic nucleus** (via the retinohypothalamic tract).

**LGN**: six layers. Layers 1–2 magnocellular (motion, contrast), 3–6 parvocellular (color, detail), with koniocellular layers between. Contralateral eye → layers 1, 4, 6; ipsilateral → 2, 3, 5. Eye inputs remain segregated until V1.

**Optic radiations (geniculocalcarine tract)**:
- **Meyer's loop**: inferior fibers sweep anteriorly around the temporal horn of the lateral ventricle, carrying the **contralateral superior** visual quadrant to the **lower bank** of the calcarine fissure (lingual gyrus).
- **Parietal (dorsal) fibers**: carry the **contralateral inferior** quadrant to the **upper bank** (cuneus).

**V1 (striate cortex, area 17)**: retinotopic, with the macula at the occipital pole occupying a disproportionately large area (**cortical magnification**). The peripheral field is anterior along the calcarine fissure; the far temporal crescent of each field is monocular, represented most anteriorly.

**Extrastriate cortex**: V2, V3, **V4** (color; lesions cause cerebral achromatopsia), **MT/V5** (motion; lesions cause akinetopsia), **fusiform face area** (prosopagnosia when damaged). **Dorsal stream** (occipito-parietal) for where and how; **ventral stream** (occipito-temporal) for what.

**Blood supply**: optic radiations mainly MCA (and anterior choroidal for the tract and LGN); V1 by the **PCA**, with the occipital pole often receiving collateral MCA supply.
levels.phd:
**Cortical computation.** Hubel and Wiesel discovered orientation-selective simple and complex cells in V1, ocular dominance columns, and the critical period: monocular deprivation in kittens during early life permanently shifts V1 toward the open eye. This is the neural basis of **amblyopia**, which is why childhood strabismus and anisometropia must be treated early, and why recent work on reopening plasticity in adults (perceptual learning, dichoptic training, pharmacological manipulation of perineuronal nets) is clinically important.

**Two streams, refined.** Ungerleider and Mishkin's what/where model was reframed by Goodale and Milner as vision-for-perception (ventral) versus vision-for-action (dorsal). Patient DF, with ventral stream damage (visual form agnosia), could not report a slot's orientation yet posted a card through it accurately. Optic ataxia from dorsal damage shows the reverse dissociation. Modern work emphasizes extensive cross-talk and a third lateral stream for social perception.

**Blindsight.** Patients with V1 lesions can detect, localize and discriminate motion in their "blind" field above chance without awareness. Pathways bypassing V1 (retina → superior colliculus → pulvinar → MT, and direct koniocellular LGN → MT projections) mediate it, showing that visual processing and visual awareness are dissociable.

**Retinotopic mapping** with fMRI population receptive field methods delineates more than 20 visual areas in humans. The log-polar transformation from retina to V1 means a small foveal lesion in the retina corresponds to a large cortical territory and vice versa.

**Myelination and plasticity.** The optic nerve is a classic model of CNS axon regeneration failure: inhibitory myelin proteins (Nogo, MAG, OMgp), glial scar chondroitin sulfate proteoglycans, and low intrinsic growth capacity (low mTOR activity, PTEN, SOCS3) prevent regrowth. Combined PTEN deletion and other manipulations allow long-distance optic nerve regeneration in rodents, a leading paradigm for CNS repair.

**Achiasmia and albinism** illustrate wiring rules: in albinism, excessive crossing of temporal fibers alters chiasmal decussation, causing nystagmus and reduced stereopsis.
levels.expert:
**Surgical anatomy you must own.**

**The chiasm and sella**: the chiasm sits above the diaphragma sellae, between the supraclinoid internal carotids, with the anterior communicating artery complex above and the third ventricle behind. A "prefixed" chiasm sits over the tuberculum sellae, a "postfixed" one over the dorsum, which changes access during surgery. Pituitary adenomas, craniopharyngiomas, tuberculum sellae meningiomas, ACom and ICA aneurysms all threaten it. The endoscopic endonasal transsphenoidal approach is the standard for most pituitary adenomas, and decompression often improves vision within days to weeks.

**Optic canal**: tuberculum sellae and anterior clinoid meningiomas extend into the canal; unroofing the canal (anterior clinoidectomy) is part of protecting the nerve. Traumatic optic neuropathy after facial or frontal impacts is usually managed conservatively; high-dose steroids were associated with harm in head-injured patients (CRASH), and canal decompression has no proven benefit for most cases.

**Meyer's loop**: during anterior temporal lobectomy for epilepsy, Meyer's loop fibers can be cut, causing a contralateral superior quadrantanopia. The loop reaches variably forward, roughly a few centimeters behind the temporal pole. Tractography-guided surgery and laser ablation reduce the risk, and the deficit can affect driving eligibility, so preoperative counseling matters.

**Optic radiations in glioma surgery**: radiations run along the lateral wall of the temporal and occipital horns; transcortical approaches to the atrium can damage them. Awake mapping with visual tasks and DTI help preserve them.

**Occipital lobe**: occipital resections or PCA strokes cause contralateral homonymous hemianopia, often with macular sparing.

**Monitoring**: visual evoked potentials during surgery are less reliable than SSEPs or MEPs under anesthesia, so careful anatomical technique remains the main protection.

**Pitfall**: always do formal visual fields before and after surgery near the visual pathway. Patients often don't notice a quadrantanopia or even a hemianopia, and the deficit discovered later is attributed to the operation.

keyPoints: Retina → optic nerve → chiasm → optic tract → LGN → optic radiations → V1 (calcarine cortex)
At the chiasm, nasal retinal fibers (temporal visual field) cross; temporal fibers stay ipsilateral
Each optic tract carries the contralateral visual field from both eyes
Meyer's loop (temporal) = contralateral superior quadrant; parietal radiations = inferior quadrant
Macula is represented at the occipital pole, with large cortical magnification
Dorsal stream = where/how (parietal); ventral stream = what (temporal; V4 color, fusiform faces)

lessons.title: Visual Field Defects

levels.kid:
Doctors can play a detective game with your eyes. They ask you to look at their nose and say when you see their wiggling finger off to the side.

If part of what you see is missing, that missing piece is a clue. It tells the doctor where along the eye-to-brain road something is wrong.

If one whole eye can't see, the problem is near that eye. If both eyes lose their outside edges, something may be pressing on the X-shaped crossing. If both eyes lose the same side, the problem is farther back in the brain.

It's like finding which road is blocked by seeing which houses lost their mail!
levels.hs:
Your **visual field** is everything you can see while looking straight ahead. Doctors describe it from the **patient's** point of view and test each eye separately.

Where the damage is predicts the pattern of loss:
- **Optic nerve** (in front of the chiasm): vision loss in **one eye** only.
- **Optic chiasm**: loss of both **outer** (temporal) halves, called **bitemporal hemianopia**. The classic cause is a **pituitary tumor** pressing up on the crossing fibers.
- **Optic tract, radiations or occipital cortex** (behind the chiasm): loss of the **same side** of the field in **both eyes**, called **homonymous hemianopia**. A right-sided lesion causes loss of the left field.
- **Temporal lobe (Meyer's loop)**: loss of the upper quarter on the opposite side in both eyes, nicknamed "**pie in the sky**".
- **Parietal lobe**: loss of the lower quarter on the opposite side, "**pie on the floor**".
- **Occipital stroke**: homonymous hemianopia, often with the center of vision spared (**macular sparing**) because the occipital pole has a backup blood supply.

Simple rule: a defect in **one eye** means the problem is **in front of** the chiasm. A defect **across the middle** in both eyes means the chiasm or behind.

Doctors test fields at the bedside by **confrontation** and more precisely with **automated perimetry**.
levels.college:
**Principles**: fields are recorded from the patient's view; the right eye's field is drawn on the right. Retinal and visual field coordinates are inverted and reversed. Defects that respect the **vertical meridian** indicate chiasmal or retrochiasmal lesions; defects that respect the **horizontal meridian** suggest retinal vascular or optic nerve (glaucoma, ischemic optic neuropathy) disease.

**Lesion-defect map**:
1. **Optic nerve**: ipsilateral monocular loss; **central scotoma** (optic neuritis), altitudinal defect (anterior ischemic optic neuropathy), with a **relative afferent pupillary defect (RAPD)**.
2. **Junction of optic nerve and chiasm**: **junctional scotoma**: ipsilateral central scotoma plus a contralateral superotemporal defect.
3. **Chiasm (midline)**: **bitemporal hemianopia**. Pituitary macroadenomas compress from below, affecting inferior crossing fibers first, giving **superior** bitemporal quadrantanopia initially. Craniopharyngiomas, often from above, may begin with inferior defects.
4. **Optic tract**: contralateral **incongruous** homonymous hemianopia, often with an RAPD in the contralateral eye and later optic atrophy.
5. **Meyer's loop (temporal)**: contralateral **superior** homonymous quadrantanopia.
6. **Parietal radiations**: contralateral **inferior** homonymous quadrantanopia.
7. **Occipital cortex (PCA)**: contralateral **congruous** homonymous hemianopia, often with **macular sparing**; isolated occipital pole lesions cause small central homonymous scotomas.
8. **Bilateral occipital**: cortical blindness with normal pupils; **Anton syndrome** if the patient denies blindness.

**Congruity**: the more posterior the lesion, the more identical (congruous) the defects in the two eyes, because fibers from corresponding retinal points lie closer together posteriorly.

**Testing**: confrontation (finger counting in each quadrant, red target comparison), Amsler grid (central), **automated static perimetry** (Humphrey), kinetic perimetry (Goldmann).

**Enlarged blind spot**: papilledema. **Arcuate defects and nasal step**: glaucoma.
levels.phd:
**Why the defects look the way they do.** Retinotopy is preserved through every relay, but fiber arrangement changes. In the anterior optic tract, fibers from corresponding points of the two eyes are not yet aligned, so tract lesions produce incongruous defects. By V1, inputs from corresponding points converge on neighboring ocular dominance columns, so cortical lesions produce near-perfectly congruous defects.

**Wilbrand's knee revisited.** The junctional scotoma was explained by inferonasal crossing fibers looping briefly into the contralateral optic nerve (Wilbrand's knee). Horton's monkey studies suggested the knee is an artifact of long-term enucleation, implying junctional scotomas arise from direct compression of the chiasm's anterior angle. The clinical sign remains valid even if the anatomy is debated.

**Macular sparing** has competing explanations: dual blood supply of the occipital pole (PCA plus MCA collaterals), bilateral foveal representation (disputed by split-fovea studies), and fixation shifts during testing. Most likely the vascular explanation predominates, with testing artifacts contributing.

**Hemifield slide and nonseeing-field phenomena.** Bitemporal hemianopia can cause diplopia without ocular motor palsy, because the two remaining nasal hemifields lack overlapping stimuli to lock binocular fusion: the hemifields drift apart (hemifield slide). Homonymous hemianopia affects reading differently by side: right hemianopia (text ahead) slows reading more than left in left-to-right languages.

**Plasticity and rehabilitation.** Spontaneous field recovery after occipital stroke occurs mostly in the first months. Visual restoration training remains controversial; compensatory saccadic training (exploring into the blind field) has better evidence. Studies of perceptual learning in the blind field show improvements in motion discrimination, raising questions about residual V1 islands versus extrastriate routes.

**Quantitation.** Structure-function mapping relates perimetry to OCT retinal layer thickness. Band atrophy (a horizontal "bow-tie" pattern) of the optic disc after chiasmal compression reflects loss of nasal fibers entering the disc nasally and temporally.
levels.expert:
**A pituitary patient, start to finish.**
- Presentation: often gradual peripheral vision loss the patient doesn't notice, headaches, or hormonal symptoms (amenorrhea-galactorrhea, acromegaly, Cushing features, hypopituitarism).
- Exam: formal automated fields in both eyes, acuity, color vision, fundoscopy (band atrophy suggests chronic compression), and pupils.
- Workup: pituitary MRI with contrast; full endocrine panel. **Check prolactin before surgery**: a **prolactinoma**, even with field loss, is usually treated first with dopamine agonists (such as cabergoline), which shrink the tumor and often restore vision. Beware the "hook effect" giving falsely low prolactin with very large tumors; ask the lab to dilute.
- Nonfunctioning macroadenoma with chiasmal compression: endoscopic endonasal transsphenoidal resection.
- **Pituitary apoplexy**: sudden severe headache, visual loss, ophthalmoplegia and possible adrenal crisis from hemorrhage or infarction of a tumor. Give **stress-dose steroids** urgently; urgent decompression for severe or worsening vision.

**Other neurosurgical field patterns:**
- Tuberculum sellae meningioma: asymmetric loss starting in one eye (optic nerve) plus temporal defect in the other.
- Supraclinoid carotid aneurysm compressing the lateral chiasm: nasal field defect in the ipsilateral eye.
- Temporal lobectomy: superior quadrantanopia; check driving standards before telling a patient they can drive.
- Hydrocephalus with a dilated third ventricle compressing the chiasm from above.

**Distinguishing neuro from eye causes**: vertical meridian = brain or chiasm; horizontal meridian or arcuate = eye or optic nerve head (glaucoma, ischemic optic neuropathy, branch retinal vascular occlusion).

**Pitfalls**:
- A "bitemporal" defect from tilted discs or uncorrected refractive error crosses the vertical meridian; repeat with correction before ordering urgent imaging.
- Homonymous hemianopia patients often complain of "trouble in one eye" (the eye on the side of the field loss, which has the larger temporal field). Test both eyes before blaming the eye.
- Always document fields before surgery near the visual pathway; it protects the patient and you.

keyPoints: Monocular defect = optic nerve (in front of the chiasm); bilateral defects respecting the vertical meridian = chiasm or behind
Chiasm (pituitary tumor) → bitemporal hemianopia; adenomas from below hit superior fields first
Optic tract/radiation/occipital lesion → contralateral homonymous hemianopia
Meyer's loop (temporal) → contralateral superior quadrantanopia ('pie in the sky'); parietal → inferior ('pie on the floor')
Occipital (PCA) stroke → congruous homonymous hemianopia with macular sparing
Check prolactin before pituitary surgery: prolactinomas are treated medically first

test.q: A pituitary tumor pressing on the chiasm classically causes:
choices: Central scotoma in both eyes only
test.explain: Crossing nasal fibers carry temporal fields; compressing them removes both temporal fields.

test.q: Loss of the left visual field in both eyes (left homonymous hemianopia) localizes to the:
choices: Right optic tract, radiations or occipital lobe
test.explain: Retrochiasmal lesions cause contralateral field loss; right-sided damage removes the left field.

test.q: Complete loss of vision in the right eye only localizes to the:
test.explain: A monocular defect means the lesion is in front of the chiasm.

test.q: 'Pie in the sky' (contralateral superior quadrantanopia) comes from a lesion in the:
test.explain: Meyer's loop carries the superior field through the temporal lobe.

test.q: 'Pie on the floor' (contralateral inferior quadrantanopia) points to the:
test.explain: Dorsal radiations through the parietal lobe carry the inferior field.

test.q: Macular sparing is typical of which lesion?
test.explain: The occipital pole often has collateral MCA supply.

test.q: Because pituitary adenomas compress the chiasm from below, the earliest defect is often:
test.explain: Inferior crossing fibers carry the superior temporal fields.

test.q: Which defect pattern suggests eye disease such as glaucoma rather than a brain lesion?
choices: Arcuate defect respecting the horizontal meridian
test.explain: Retinal nerve fiber layer arrangement makes glaucoma respect the horizontal meridian.

test.q: Which tumor should be treated with medication first even if it causes field loss?
test.explain: Dopamine agonists shrink most prolactinomas and can restore vision.

test.q: Loss of the same half of the field in both eyes is called ___ hemianopia.
test.explain: Homonymous means the same side in both eyes.

test.q: Loss of both outer (temporal) half-fields is called?
test.explain: Classic for chiasmal compression.

test.q: Posterior (occipital) lesions produce more ___ defects, nearly identical in both eyes.
test.explain: Corresponding fibers lie closer together posteriorly.

test.q: Bedside visual field testing facing the patient is called ___ testing.
test.explain: Confrontation fields compare the patient's field with the examiner's.

kidTest.q: The doctor asks you to look at their nose and spot their:
kidTest.explain: That tests your side vision.

kidTest.q: A missing piece of what you see is a:
kidTest.explain: It tells the doctor where the problem is.

kidTest.q: If one whole eye can't see, the problem is near:
kidTest.explain: One-eye problems are near that eye.

kidTest.q: If both eyes lose the same side, the problem is:
kidTest.explain: Same-side loss in both eyes means behind the crossing.

kidTest.q: The doctor plays a ___ game to find the problem.
kidTest.explain: Finding clues in what you can see.

kidTest.q: You should test each eye:
kidTest.explain: Each eye is tested separately.

advancedTest.q: Right eye central scotoma plus a left eye superotemporal defect localizes to the:
choices: Junction of the right optic nerve and chiasm
advancedTest.explain: That is a junctional scotoma from anterior chiasmal compression on the right.

advancedTest.q: A patient with a large pituitary mass has a mildly elevated prolactin. A key lab pitfall:
choices: Hook effect causing falsely low prolactin; request dilution
Prolactin is always normal in adenomas
advancedTest.explain: Huge prolactin concentrations saturate the assay; dilution reveals true levels. Mild elevation may also be stalk effect.

advancedTest.q: Sudden severe headache, vision loss and ophthalmoplegia in a patient with a pituitary adenoma. First priority:
choices: Stress-dose corticosteroids and urgent neurosurgical evaluation
advancedTest.explain: Pituitary apoplexy risks adrenal crisis; steroids are lifesaving, and decompression rescues vision.

advancedTest.q: A left optic tract lesion typically produces an RAPD in the:
advancedTest.explain: The tract carries more crossed fibers from the contralateral (right) eye's nasal retina, so the right eye shows the RAPD.

lessons.title: Pupils & Gaze Control

levels.kid:
Look in a mirror and shine a light near your eye. The black dot in the middle, your pupil, gets smaller! In the dark, it gets bigger to let more light in. It's like a camera opening and closing.

Shine a light in one eye and BOTH pupils shrink. They're a team.

Your eyes also move together like dance partners. When you look to the right, one eye moves out and the other moves in, at exactly the same time. Special centers deep in your brain keep them in step.

Doctors check pupils and eye movements to see if the brain is okay, especially after someone bumps their head.
levels.hs:
**Pupil size** is controlled by two muscles in the iris:
- **Sphincter pupillae** (constricts) controlled by the **parasympathetic** system through cranial nerve **III**
- **Dilator pupillae** (dilates) controlled by the **sympathetic** system

**Pupillary light reflex**: light in one eye → optic nerve → **pretectal area** of the midbrain → both **Edinger-Westphal nuclei** → CN III on both sides → both pupils constrict. The pupil in the lit eye constricts (**direct** response) and so does the other (**consensual** response).

**Near response**: looking at something close makes the eyes converge, the lenses thicken (accommodation) and the pupils constrict.

Important pupil problems:
- **"Blown" pupil**: a large pupil that doesn't react, from compression of CN III, for example by a brain swelling or bleed pushing the temporal lobe down (**uncal herniation**) or an aneurysm. A neurosurgical emergency.
- **Horner syndrome**: small pupil, droopy eyelid and reduced sweating on one side from damage to the sympathetic pathway.

**Eye movements** use six muscles per eye, controlled by three nerves:
- **CN III**: most muscles, plus lifting the eyelid
- **CN IV**: superior oblique
- **CN VI**: lateral rectus (moves the eye outward)

The **pons** has a horizontal gaze center that coordinates both eyes. The **medial longitudinal fasciculus (MLF)** links the nuclei so the eyes move together. Damage to the MLF, often from multiple sclerosis, makes one eye fail to move inward.
levels.college:
**Light reflex pathway**: retinal ganglion cells (including melanopsin cells) → optic nerve and tract → **pretectal olivary nucleus** → bilateral projections (via posterior commissure) → **Edinger-Westphal nuclei** → preganglionic parasympathetic fibers in **CN III** → **ciliary ganglion** → short ciliary nerves → sphincter pupillae.

**Swinging flashlight test**: in an **afferent** defect (optic nerve), both pupils dilate when the light swings to the affected eye: a **relative afferent pupillary defect (RAPD, Marcus Gunn pupil)**. Afferent defects never cause anisocoria.

**Sympathetic pathway (3 neurons)**: hypothalamus → descends through brainstem and cervical cord → **ciliospinal center** (C8–T2) → preganglionic fibers exit at T1, ascend over the lung apex in the sympathetic chain → **superior cervical ganglion** → postganglionic fibers travel with the **internal carotid artery** → long ciliary nerves to the dilator and fibers to **Müller's muscle** (eyelid).
**Horner syndrome**: miosis, mild ptosis, anhidrosis (pattern varies by lesion site). Causes: lateral medullary stroke, **Pancoast tumor**, **carotid dissection** (painful Horner).

**Anisocoria rules**: greater in the dark → the small pupil is abnormal (Horner); greater in light → the large pupil is abnormal (CN III palsy, Adie tonic pupil, pharmacologic dilation).

**Pupil syndromes**:
- **Compressive CN III palsy**: parasympathetic fibers lie superficially on the nerve, so compression (posterior communicating artery aneurysm, uncal herniation) dilates the pupil early. Microvascular (diabetic) palsies usually spare the pupil.
- **Argyll Robertson pupils** (neurosyphilis): small, irregular, accommodate but don't react to light (light-near dissociation).

**Gaze control**:
- **Horizontal**: frontal eye field (area 8) → contralateral **PPRF** → **abducens nucleus**, which drives the ipsilateral lateral rectus and sends internuclear axons up the contralateral **MLF** to the medial rectus subnucleus of CN III.
- **INO** (MLF lesion): ipsilateral adduction failure with nystagmus of the abducting eye; convergence preserved. Bilateral INO in a young adult = multiple sclerosis.
- **Vertical**: **riMLF** in the midbrain. **Parinaud (dorsal midbrain) syndrome**: upgaze palsy, light-near dissociation, convergence-retraction nystagmus, eyelid retraction.
- **Gaze deviation**: destructive frontal lesions → eyes deviate toward the lesion; pontine lesions → away from the lesion; seizure focus → away from the focus.
levels.phd:
**Saccade generation.** Burst neurons in the PPRF (horizontal) and riMLF (vertical) fire high-frequency bursts that produce the pulse of force overcoming orbital viscosity; tonic neurons supply the step that holds the eye in place. The step is produced by a **neural integrator**: the nucleus prepositus hypoglossi and medial vestibular nucleus for horizontal gaze and the interstitial nucleus of Cajal for vertical gaze, mathematically integrating velocity commands into position signals. A leaky integrator causes gaze-evoked nystagmus: the eyes drift back to center and correct with saccades. **Omnipause neurons** in the nucleus raphe interpositus inhibit burst neurons between saccades; their dysfunction may underlie opsoclonus.

**Superior colliculus** holds a motor map of saccade vectors with a winner-take-all population code; frontal eye field and colliculus each can generate saccades, so lesions of either alone produce limited permanent deficits, while combined lesions abolish visually guided saccades.

**Cerebellar calibration.** The dorsal vermis and fastigial nucleus adapt saccade amplitude (saccadic adaptation paradigms), while the flocculus and paraflocculus maintain pursuit, gaze holding and VOR gain. Floccular lesions produce downbeat nystagmus and impaired pursuit; fastigial lesions cause saccadic dysmetria.

**Vestibulo-ocular reflex.** A three-neuron arc (vestibular afferent → vestibular nucleus → ocular motor nucleus) produces compensatory eye movements with a latency of only several milliseconds, among the fastest reflexes in the body. The **head impulse test** exploits it: a corrective saccade after a rapid head turn indicates peripheral vestibular loss, a component of the HINTS exam distinguishing vestibular neuritis from posterior circulation stroke.

**Pupillary physiology.** Melanopsin ipRGCs drive the sustained component of pupil constriction and post-illumination pupil response, which persists in rod-cone degeneration. Pupil diameter also tracks locus coeruleus activity and cognitive load, making pupillometry a window into arousal; quantitative automated pupillometry (constriction velocity and the Neurological Pupil index) outperforms subjective assessment in detecting early herniation.
levels.expert:
**Pupils in the neurosurgical patient** are a vital sign.

- **Uncal (transtentorial) herniation**: an expanding supratentorial mass pushes the uncus over the tentorial edge, compressing CN III: first a sluggish, then dilated unreactive pupil, usually **ipsilateral** to the mass, followed by decreased consciousness and contralateral hemiparesis. **Kernohan's notch** phenomenon (contralateral peduncle compressed against the tentorium) produces hemiparesis **ipsilateral** to the mass, a false localizing sign.
- A new fixed dilated pupil in a head-injured patient demands immediate action: airway, temporary hyperventilation as a bridge, hyperosmolar therapy (mannitol or hypertonic saline), urgent CT and, for an extra-axial hematoma, emergency evacuation or decompressive craniectomy.
- **Pupil-involving third nerve palsy** in an awake patient = **posterior communicating artery aneurysm until proven otherwise**: urgent CTA or catheter angiography, because rupture is imminent risk. Treat by clipping or endovascular coiling.
- **CN VI palsy** can be a false localizing sign of raised ICP due to its long intracranial course.
- **Bilateral small pinpoint pupils**: pontine hemorrhage or opioid toxicity. **Bilateral fixed mid-sized pupils**: midbrain injury or brain death.
- Confounders: atropine, nebulized ipratropium (unilateral dilation if it drifts into one eye), prior eye surgery, artificial eyes, dilating drops for fundoscopy.

**Brain death examination** includes absent pupillary light reflexes, absent corneal reflexes, absent **oculocephalic** (doll's eyes) and **oculovestibular** (cold caloric) responses, absent cough and gag, and apnea testing, after excluding confounders.

**Gaze in coma**: eyes deviated toward a hemispheric lesion (away from the hemiparesis) suggest a destructive cortical lesion; eyes deviated away from the lesion toward the hemiparesis suggest a pontine lesion or an ongoing seizure. Skew deviation suggests a brainstem lesion.

**Dorsal midbrain syndrome in a child with hydrocephalus or a pineal mass**: upgaze palsy and light-near dissociation; it can signal **shunt failure**, an emergency in a shunted patient.

**Pitfall**: never assume a dilated pupil is from drops without proof; document any drug given and recheck.

keyPoints: Light reflex: retina → optic nerve → pretectum → bilateral Edinger-Westphal → CN III → ciliary ganglion → sphincter (direct + consensual)
RAPD (swinging flashlight) = afferent optic nerve defect; afferent defects don't cause anisocoria
Sympathetic: hypothalamus → C8–T2 → superior cervical ganglion → along internal carotid; Horner = ptosis, miosis, anhidrosis
Pupil-involving CN III palsy = compression (PComm aneurysm, uncal herniation) until proven otherwise
Horizontal gaze: FEF → contralateral PPRF → abducens nucleus → MLF → contralateral medial rectus; MLF lesion = INO
Parinaud (dorsal midbrain): upgaze palsy, light-near dissociation, convergence-retraction nystagmus

test.q: Which nerve carries the parasympathetic fibers that constrict the pupil?
test.explain: Edinger-Westphal fibers travel in CN III to the ciliary ganglion.

test.q: Light shone in the right eye makes the left pupil constrict too. This is the:
test.explain: Bilateral pretectal projections produce the consensual response.

test.q: In the swinging flashlight test, both pupils dilate when the light moves to the left eye. This suggests:
test.explain: That is a left RAPD (Marcus Gunn pupil).

test.q: Ptosis, a small pupil and reduced sweating on one side suggest:
test.explain: Horner syndrome reflects interrupted sympathetic supply.

test.q: A painful Horner syndrome after neck trauma should raise concern for:
test.explain: Postganglionic fibers run with the internal carotid; dissection is a stroke risk.

test.q: A dilated unreactive pupil with ptosis and an eye turned 'down and out' in a headache patient suggests:
choices: Compressive CN III palsy, e.g., posterior communicating artery aneurysm
test.explain: Pupillary fibers are superficial and affected early by compression.

test.q: The lateral rectus is supplied by:
test.explain: CN VI (abducens) abducts the eye.

test.q: A lesion of the medial longitudinal fasciculus causes:
test.explain: INO: impaired adduction of the ipsilateral eye with nystagmus of the abducting eye.

test.q: Pupils that react to near but not to light, small and irregular, suggest:
test.explain: Light-near dissociation with small irregular pupils is classic for neurosyphilis.

test.q: Upgaze palsy with light-near dissociation from a pineal tumor is ___ syndrome.
test.explain: Parinaud (dorsal midbrain) syndrome.

test.q: Which cranial nerve supplies the superior oblique muscle? (Roman numeral or number)
test.explain: The trochlear nerve (CN IV) supplies the superior oblique.

test.q: The horizontal gaze center in the pons is the paramedian pontine ___ formation.
test.explain: PPRF = paramedian pontine reticular formation.

test.q: What does RAPD stand for? (four words)
test.explain: An RAPD indicates asymmetric optic nerve or severe retinal disease.

kidTest.q: In bright light, your pupil gets:
kidTest.explain: Pupils shrink in bright light.

kidTest.q: In the dark, your pupil gets:
kidTest.explain: Bigger pupils let in more light.

kidTest.q: Light in one eye makes:
kidTest.explain: The pupils are a team.

kidTest.q: Your eyes move together like:
kidTest.explain: Brain centers keep them in step.

kidTest.q: The black dot in the middle of your eye is the ___.
kidTest.explain: The pupil lets light in.

kidTest.q: Doctors check pupils after someone:
kidTest.explain: Pupils help show if the brain is okay.

advancedTest.q: A patient with a right acute subdural hematoma has a dilated right pupil and RIGHT-sided hemiparesis. The hemiparesis is best explained by:
choices: Kernohan's notch: left cerebral peduncle compressed against the tentorium
advancedTest.explain: Kernohan's phenomenon gives a false localizing hemiparesis ipsilateral to the mass.

advancedTest.q: Anisocoria that is greater in the dark indicates that:
choices: The smaller pupil is abnormal (e.g., Horner)
advancedTest.explain: A Horner pupil fails to dilate in darkness, so the difference grows in the dark.

advancedTest.q: Bilateral INO in a 25-year-old most strongly suggests:
advancedTest.explain: Demyelination of both MLFs is classic for MS; unilateral INO in older adults is more often a stroke.

advancedTest.q: Eyes deviated to the right with left hemiparesis in an unresponsive patient (no seizure) suggests:
advancedTest.explain: Destructive hemispheric lesions turn the eyes toward the lesion and away from the hemiparesis.

advancedTest.q: Increasing headache, upgaze palsy and light-near dissociation in a child with a VP shunt suggest:
advancedTest.explain: Dorsal midbrain compression from a dilated third ventricle/aqueduct signals shunt failure; urgent evaluation.
